claim: Most of the cholesterol in the plasma membranes (PMs) of animal cells is sequestered through interactions with phospholipids and transmembrane domains of proteins.
source: Most of the cholesterol in the plasma membranes (PMs) of animal cells is sequestered through interactions with phospholipids and transmembrane domains of proteins.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about cholesterol organization in plasma membranes.

claim: As cholesterol concentration rises above the PM's sequestration capacity, a new pool of cholesterol, called accessible cholesterol, emerges.
source: However, as cholesterol concentration rises above the PM's sequestration capacity, a new pool of cholesterol, called accessible cholesterol, emerges.
evidence: This is based on established scientific understanding of cholesterol organization in membranes.

claim: The transport of accessible cholesterol between the PM and the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is critical to maintain cholesterol homeostasis.
source: The transport of accessible cholesterol between the PM and the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is critical to maintain cholesterol homeostasis.
evidence: This is a statement based on established scientific knowledge about cholesterol homeostasis.

claim: The accessible cholesterol pathway has been implicated in the suppression of both bacterial and viral pathogens by immunomodulatory oxysterols.
source: This pathway has also been implicated in the suppression of both bacterial and viral pathogens by immunomodulatory oxysterols.
evidence: This statement references prior research findings without specific citations in this sentence.

claim: 25HC-mediated activation of ACAT in the ER creates an imbalance in the equilibrium distribution of accessible cholesterol between the ER and PM.
source: We show that 25HC-mediated activation of acyl coenzyme A: cholesterol acyltransferase (ACAT) in the ER creates an imbalance in the equilibrium distribution of accessible cholesterol between the ER and PM.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The imbalance in accessible cholesterol distribution triggers the rapid internalization of accessible cholesterol from the PM.
source: This imbalance triggers the rapid internalization of accessible cholesterol from the PM, and this depletion is sustained for long periods of time through 25HC-mediated suppression of SREBPs and continued activation of ACAT.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Depletion of accessible PM cholesterol is sustained for long periods of time through 25HC-mediated suppression of SREBPs and continued activation of ACAT.
source: This imbalance triggers the rapid internalization of accessible cholesterol from the PM, and this depletion is sustained for long periods of time through 25HC-mediated suppression of SREBPs and continued activation of ACAT.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: 25HC failed to suppress Zika virus infection in ACAT-deficient cells.
source: In support of a physiological role for this mechanism, 25HC failed to suppress Zika virus and human coronavirus infection in ACAT-deficient cells, and Listeria monocytogenes infection in ACAT-deficient cells and mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: 25HC failed to suppress human coronavirus infection in ACAT-deficient cells.
source: In support of a physiological role for this mechanism, 25HC failed to suppress Zika virus and human coronavirus infection in ACAT-deficient cells, and Listeria monocytogenes infection in ACAT-deficient cells and mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: 25HC failed to suppress Listeria monocytogenes infection in ACAT-deficient cells.
source: In support of a physiological role for this mechanism, 25HC failed to suppress Zika virus and human coronavirus infection in ACAT-deficient cells, and Listeria monocytogenes infection in ACAT-deficient cells and mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: 25HC failed to suppress Listeria monocytogenes infection in ACAT-deficient mice.
source: In support of a physiological role for this mechanism, 25HC failed to suppress Zika virus and human coronavirus infection in ACAT-deficient cells, and Listeria monocytogenes infection in ACAT-deficient cells and mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Selective depletion of accessible PM cholesterol triggered by ACAT activation and sustained through SREBP suppression underpins the immunological activities of 25HC and a functionally related class of oxysterols.
source: We propose that selective depletion of accessible PM cholesterol triggered by ACAT activation and sustained through SREBP suppression underpins the immunological activities of 25HC and a functionally related class of oxysterols.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings of the study.

claim: Cholesterol is an essential component of the membranes of animal cells and its levels are tightly regulated by multiple feedback mechanisms that control its production, uptake, and intracellular distribution.
source: Cholesterol is an essential component of the membranes of animal cells and its levels are tightly regulated by multiple feedback mechanisms that control its production, uptake, and intracellular distribution (Brown et al., 2018; Luo et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Dysregulation of cellular cholesterol homeostasis is implicated in many human diseases ranging from atherosclerosis to cancer.
source: Dysregulation of cellular cholesterol homeostasis is implicated in many human diseases ranging from atherosclerosis to cancer (Goldstein and Brown, 2015; Shimano and Sato, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There is growing evidence that membrane cholesterol modulation plays key roles in host defense against bacterial and viral pathogens.
source: There is also growing evidence that membrane cholesterol modulation plays key roles in host defense against bacterial and viral pathogens (Cyster et al., 2014; Abrams et al., 2020a; Zhou et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Most of a mammalian cell's cholesterol is concentrated in the plasma membrane (PM), where the molecule makes up 40–50% of the total lipids.
source: Most of a mammalian cell's cholesterol is concentrated in the plasma membrane (PM), where the molecule makes up 40–50% of the total lipids (van Meer et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The steady state levels of PM cholesterol are regulated by balancing the flow of cholesterol into and out of the PM.
source: The steady state levels of PM cholesterol are regulated by balancing the flow of cholesterol into and out of the PM.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge.

claim: Inflows to the PM originate from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) where cholesterol is synthesized and from lysosomes where cholesterol is liberated from low-density lipoproteins (LDL).
source: Inflows to the PM originate from two locations – (i) the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) where cholesterol is synthesized; and (ii) lysosomes where cholesterol is liberated from low-density lipoproteins (LDL) that bind to LDL receptors on the PM and are internalized by receptor-mediated endocytosis (Brown and Goldstein, 1986).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Upon arrival at the PM, incoming cholesterol forms complexes with sphingomyelin (SM) and other PM phospholipids, which imparts the PM with structural properties required for proper cellular function and growth.
source: Upon arrival at the PM from these locations, the incoming cholesterol forms complexes with sphingomyelin (SM) and other PM phospholipids, which imparts the PM with structural properties required for proper cellular function and growth (Simons and Ikonen, 2000; McConnell and Radhakrishnan, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Cholesterol in excess of the sequestering capacity of PM phospholipids forms a pool that has been termed 'accessible cholesterol'.
source: Cholesterol in excess of the sequestering capacity of PM phospholipids forms a pool that has been termed 'accessible cholesterol' (Das et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Expansion of the accessible cholesterol pool signals cholesterol overaccumulation and triggers flow of accessible cholesterol out of the cell by PM cholesterol efflux proteins or into the cell by cholesterol transporters that move the lipid to organelles such as the ER.
source: Expansion of this pool signals cholesterol overaccumulation and triggers flow of accessible cholesterol out of the cell by PM cholesterol efflux proteins (Venkateswaran et al., 2000; Repa and Mangelsdorf, 2000), or into the cell by cholesterol transporters that move the lipid to organelles such as the ER (Lange et al., 2004; Infante and Radhakrishnan, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The accessible cholesterol that is transported to the ER interacts with Scap, a cholesterol sensor, and ACAT, a cholesterol-modifying enzyme.
source: The accessible cholesterol that is transported to the ER interacts with two regulatory membrane proteins, a cholesterol sensor called Scap (Radhakrishnan et al., 2004; Sokolov and Radhakrishnan, 2010) and a cholesterol-modifying enzyme called acyl coenzyme A: cholesterol acyltransferase (ACAT), also designated as sterol O-acyltransferase (SOAT) (Chang et al., 2006; Xu and Tabas, 1991).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Binding of cholesterol to Scap prevents the activation of sterol regulatory element-binding proteins (SREBPs), transcription factors that upregulate genes for lipid production, including those for cholesterol synthesis and uptake.
source: Binding of cholesterol to Scap prevents the activation of sterol regulatory element-binding proteins (SREBPs), transcription factors that upregulate genes for lipid production, including those for cholesterol synthesis and uptake (Brown et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The ACAT enzyme converts some of the incoming cholesterol to cholesteryl esters for storage in cytoplasmic lipid droplets.
source: The ACAT enzyme converts some of the incoming cholesterol to cholesteryl esters for storage in cytoplasmic lipid droplets (Chang et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Accessible cholesterol in the PM can be a vulnerability as it is exploited by numerous bacteria and viruses to promote infection.
source: While accessible cholesterol in the PM plays a crucial role in maintaining cholesterol homeostasis and regulating cell growth, this pool of cholesterol can also be a vulnerability as it is exploited by numerous bacteria and viruses to promote infection (Abrams et al., 2020a; Zhou et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: An innate immune response stimulates the expression of cholesterol 25-hydroxylase (CH25H), an enzyme that attaches a hydroxyl group to the iso-octyl sidechain of cholesterol to generate 25-hydroxycholesterol (25HC).
source: The solution involves an innate immune response that stimulates the expression of cholesterol 25-hydroxylase (CH25H), an enzyme that attaches a hydroxyl group to the iso-octyl sidechain of cholesterol to generate 25-hydroxycholesterol (25HC), a potent signaling molecule (Lund et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: 25HC produced by macrophage cells in response to infection acts in a paracrine manner to induce rapid depletion of accessible cholesterol, but not cholesterol in complexes with SM, from the PMs of nearby cells.
source: 25HC produced by macrophage cells in response to infection acts in a paracrine manner to induce rapid depletion of accessible cholesterol, but not cholesterol in complexes with SM, from the PMs of nearby cells.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge from prior research.

claim: Depletion of accessible cholesterol prevents the spread of infection by bacterial pathogens such as Listeria monocytogenes and Shigella flexneri.
source: Such depletion prevents the spread of infection by bacterial pathogens such as Listeria monocytogenes and Shigella flexneri (Abrams et al., 2020a) as well as cellular infection by viruses such as SARS-CoV-2, the causative agent of COVID-19 (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Depletion of accessible cholesterol prevents cellular infection by viruses such as SARS-CoV-2, the causative agent of COVID-19.
source: Such depletion prevents the spread of infection by bacterial pathogens such as Listeria monocytogenes and Shigella flexneri (Abrams et al., 2020a) as well as cellular infection by viruses such as SARS-CoV-2, the causative agent of COVID-19 (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: 25HC acts in an autocrine manner to prevent macrophage lysis by bacterial pore-forming toxins that target accessible cholesterol in membranes.
source: In addition, 25HC acts in an autocrine manner to prevent macrophage lysis by bacterial pore-forming toxins that target accessible cholesterol in membranes (Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: 25HC binds to Insigs, which suppresses the activation of SREBPs and reduces cholesterol synthesis and uptake.
source: Establishing the mechanisms of how 25HC rapidly depletes accessible cholesterol from PMs has been complicated due to this oxysterol's actions on multiple cholesterol homeostatic pathways, including (i) binding to Insigs, which suppresses the activation of SREBPs and reduces cholesterol synthesis and uptake (Radhakrishnan et al., 2007);
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: 25HC activates Liver X receptors (LXRs), transcription factors that upregulate genes encoding proteins involved in cholesterol efflux.
source: (ii) activating Liver X receptors (LXRs), transcription factors that upregulate genes encoding proteins involved in cholesterol efflux (Venkateswaran et al., 2000; Janowski et al., 1996; Costet et al., 2000);
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: 25HC stimulates the activity of ACAT, which esterifies cholesterol.
source: and (iii) stimulating the activity of ACAT, which esterifies cholesterol (Chang et al., 1997; Brown et al., 1975).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Recent studies on 25HC's role in restricting pathogen infection have pointed to the involvement of ACAT and SREBP pathways in depleting accessible cholesterol from PMs.
source: The recent studies on 25HC's role in restricting pathogen infection (Abrams et al., 2020a; Zhou et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020) have pointed to the involvement of two of these pathways – ACAT and SREBP – in depleting accessible cholesterol from PMs;
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Treatment of CHO-K1 cells with 25HC for 4 hours depleted accessible cholesterol from PMs in a dose-dependent manner.
source: When these cells were incubated with 25HC for increasing times, ALOD4 binding declined sharply after 1 hr and was eliminated after 4 hr (Figure 1A, top panel). When treated with increasing concentrations of 25HC, ALOD4 binding was sharply reduced after treatment with 1 µM 25HC and eliminated when 25HC exceeded 2.5 µM (Figure 1B, top panel). Thus, treatment of CHO-K1 cells with 25HC rapidly depleted accessible cholesterol from PMs in a dose-dependent manner, as observed previously in other cell types (Abrams et al., 2020a; Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: ALOD4 binding to CHO-K1 cells declined sharply after 1 hr of 25HC treatment and was eliminated after 4 hr.
source: When these cells were incubated with 25HC for increasing times, ALOD4 binding declined sharply after 1 hr and was eliminated after 4 hr (Figure 1A, top panel).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: ALOD4 binding to CHO-K1 cells was sharply reduced after treatment with 1 µM 25HC and eliminated when 25HC exceeded 2.5 µM.
source: When treated with increasing concentrations of 25HC, ALOD4 binding was sharply reduced after treatment with 1 µM 25HC and eliminated when 25HC exceeded 2.5 µM (Figure 1B, top panel).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Oxysterols D, G, H, I, and J markedly reduced ALOD4 binding to CHO-K1 cells.
source: As shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, ALOD4 binding to the PMs of CHO-K1 cells was markedly reduced by treatment for 4 hr with 25HC (I), as well as oxysterols harboring hydroxyl groups at carbons 20 (D) or 27 (J). Oxysterols with hydroxyl groups at carbon 24 (G, H) partially reduced ALOD4 binding, whereas oxysterols with hydroxyl groups on carbon 22 (E, F) had no effect.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Oxysterols with hydroxyl groups at carbon 24 (G, H) partially reduced ALOD4 binding to CHO-K1 cells.
source: Oxysterols with hydroxyl groups at carbon 24 (G, H) partially reduced ALOD4 binding, whereas oxysterols with hydroxyl groups on carbon 22 (E, F) had no effect.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Oxysterols with hydroxyl groups on carbon 22 (E, F) had no effect on ALOD4 binding to CHO-K1 cells.
source: Oxysterols with hydroxyl groups at carbon 24 (G, H) partially reduced ALOD4 binding, whereas oxysterols with hydroxyl groups on carbon 22 (E, F) had no effect.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The location of the hydroxyl modification on the sterol side-chain plays a crucial role in controlling accessible PM cholesterol.
source: These data indicate that the location of the hydroxyl modification on the sterol side-chain plays a crucial role in controlling accessible PM cholesterol.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The ability of a side-chain oxysterol like 25HC to reduce ALOD4 binding required the 3β-hydroxyl group since replacement of this group with a sulfate group abolished this effect.
source: Moreover, the ability of a side-chain oxysterol like 25HC (I) to reduce ALOD4 binding required the 3β-hydroxyl group since replacement of this group with a sulfate group (K) abolished this effect.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: No reduction of ALOD4 binding was detected with oxysterols bearing hydroxyl groups on the steroid nucleus at carbons 4 (A), 7 (B), or 19 (C).
source: No reduction of ALOD4 binding was detected with oxysterols bearing hydroxyl groups on the steroid nucleus at carbons 4 (A), 7 (B), or 19 (C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Oxysterols D, G, H, I, and J had no detectable effect on the binding of Ostreolysin A (OlyA), a sensor for the SM-sequestered pool of PM cholesterol.
source: While oxysterols D, G, H, I, and J reduced ALOD4 binding in an all-or-none fashion, they had no detectable effect on the binding of Ostreolysin A (OlyA) (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), a sensor for the SM-sequestered pool of PM cholesterol (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Endapally et al., 2019a; Johnson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Microscopy imaging with fluorescent versions of ALOD4 and OlyA showed that oxysterols D, G, H, I, and J eliminated accessible cholesterol, but not SM-sequestered cholesterol, from the PMs of CHO-K1 cells.
source: In line with the immunoblot analysis in Figure 1D & E, microscopy imaging with fluorescent versions of ALOD4 (fALOD4-Neon) and OlyA (fOlyA-647) also showed that oxysterols D, G, H, I, and J eliminated accessible cholesterol, but not SM-sequestered cholesterol, from the PMs of CHO-K1 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: At the highest concentrations tested, oxysterols D, G, H, I, and J reduced ALOD4 binding by more than 65%.
source: At the highest concentrations tested, oxysterols D, G, H, I, and J reduced ALOD4 binding by more than 65%, whereas treatment with oxysterols A, B, C, E, F, or K showed no such reduction (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Treatment with oxysterols A, B, C, E, F, or K showed no reduction in ALOD4 binding at the highest concentrations tested.
source: At the highest concentrations tested, oxysterols D, G, H, I, and J reduced ALOD4 binding by more than 65%, whereas treatment with oxysterols A, B, C, E, F, or K showed no such reduction (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Oxysterols D, I, and J reduced ALOD4 binding by more than 50% within 1 hr.
source: Detailed time course analyses for the five oxysterols that markedly reduced ALOD4 binding (D, G, H, I, and J) showed that oxysterols D, I, and J reduced binding by more than 50% within 1 hr, whereas oxysterols G and H required 4 hr for a similar reduction (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Oxysterols G and H required 4 hr to reduce ALOD4 binding by more than 50%.
source: Detailed time course analyses for the five oxysterols that markedly reduced ALOD4 binding (D, G, H, I, and J) showed that oxysterols D, I, and J reduced binding by more than 50% within 1 hr, whereas oxysterols G and H required 4 hr for a similar reduction (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Selective depletion of accessible PM cholesterol within 4 hr is triggered by oxysterols harboring hydroxyl groups on the iso-octyl side chain at carbons 20 (D), 24 (G, H), 25 (I), or 27 (J).
source: Together, these data indicate that selective depletion of accessible PM cholesterol within 4 hr is triggered by oxysterols harboring hydroxyl groups on the iso-octyl side chain at carbons 20 (D), 24 (G, H), 25 (I), or 27 (J).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figures 1D and 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: No reduction in fALOD4-Neon binding to rabbit red blood cells (RBCs) was observed after treatment for 4 hr with the panel of oxysterols.
source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A and B, we observed no reduction in fALOD4-Neon binding to RBCs that were treated for 4 hr with the panel of oxysterols (Figure 1C), whereas binding was abolished by treatment with hydroxypropyl β-cyclodextrin (HPCD), a reagent that extracts cholesterol from membranes (Ohtani et al., 1989).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: fALOD4-Neon binding to rabbit red blood cells was abolished by treatment with hydroxypropyl β-cyclodextrin (HPCD), a reagent that extracts cholesterol from membranes.
source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A and B, we observed no reduction in fALOD4-Neon binding to RBCs that were treated for 4 hr with the panel of oxysterols (Figure 1C), whereas binding was abolished by treatment with hydroxypropyl β-cyclodextrin (HPCD), a reagent that extracts cholesterol from membranes (Ohtani et al., 1989).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and a citation.

claim: Reduction of ALOD4 binding to the PMs of CHO-K1 cells by oxysterols D, G, H, I, and J is not due to effects on the lipid bilayer or on ALOD4, but rather due to their effects on cholesterol homeostatic pathways.
source: These results suggest that reduction of ALOD4 binding to the PMs of CHO-K1 cells by oxysterols D, G, H, I, and J is not due to effects on the lipid bilayer or on ALOD4, but rather due to their effects on cholesterol homeostatic pathways.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Oxysterols D, G, H, I, and J stimulated a more than six-fold increase in ACAT activity in CHO-K1 cells.
source: Oxysterols D, G, H, I, and J stimulated a more than six-fold increase in ACAT activity, whereas oxysterols A, B, C, E, F, and K did not show a similar stimulatory effect (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Oxysterols A, B, C, E, F, and K did not show a similar stimulatory effect on ACAT activity as oxysterols D, G, H, I, and J.
source: Oxysterols D, G, H, I, and J stimulated a more than six-fold increase in ACAT activity, whereas oxysterols A, B, C, E, F, and K did not show a similar stimulatory effect (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The oxysterol specificity for activation of ACAT exactly matched that for the depletion of accessible cholesterol from PMs.
source: This specificity for activation of ACAT exactly matched that for the depletion of accessible cholesterol from PMs (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figures 1D and 1F.

claim: Oxysterols B, D, E, G, H, I, J, and K suppressed SREBP2 cleavage in CHO-K1 cells.
source: When the cholesterol-depleted cells were then treated with each of the oxysterols for 4 hr, we observed that oxysterols B, D, E, G, H, I, J, and K suppressed SREBP2 cleavage whereas oxysterols A, C, and F had a reduced effect (Figure 1G, lanes 2–12, and Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Oxysterols A, C, and F had a reduced effect on SREBP2 cleavage in CHO-K1 cells.
source: When the cholesterol-depleted cells were then treated with each of the oxysterols for 4 hr, we observed that oxysterols B, D, E, G, H, I, J, and K suppressed SREBP2 cleavage whereas oxysterols A, C, and F had a reduced effect (Figure 1G, lanes 2–12, and Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The oxysterol specificity profile for SREBP2 suppression did not match that for depletion of accessible cholesterol from PMs.
source: This specificity profile did not match that for depletion of accessible cholesterol from PMs (see summary table in Figure 1H).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figures 1D and 1G, summarized in Figure 1H.

claim: Oxysterols B, E, and K suppressed SREBP2 cleavage but were unable to reduce ALOD4 binding, suggesting that SREBP2 suppression does not drive the rapid depletion of accessible cholesterol from PMs.
source: In particular, oxysterols B, E, and K suppressed SREBP2 cleavage but were unable to reduce ALOD4 binding (Figure 1D), suggesting that SREBP2 suppression does not drive the rapid depletion of accessible cholesterol from PMs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figures 1D and 1G.

claim: Oxysterols A, B, E, G, H, I, and J activate LXRs.
source: These studies showed that oxysterols A, B, E, G, H, I, and J activate LXRs, whereas oxysterols F and K had no such activating effect (see summary table in Figure 1H).
evidence: This statement is based on extensive previous literature cited in the text.

claim: Oxysterols F and K had no activating effect on LXRs.
source: These studies showed that oxysterols A, B, E, G, H, I, and J activate LXRs, whereas oxysterols F and K had no such activating effect (see summary table in Figure 1H).
evidence: This statement is based on extensive previous literature cited in the text.

claim: The oxysterol specificity for LXR activation did not match that for reduction in ALOD4 binding.
source: Similar to results with SREBP2, the oxysterol specificity for LXR activation also did not match that for reduction in ALOD4 binding.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data and literature review summarized in Figure 1H.

claim: ACAT1-deficient CHO-K1 cells (ACAT1 KO) had undetectable levels of ACAT1 protein.
source: The resulting ACAT1-deficient cells, hereafter designated as ACAT1 knockout (KO) cells, had undetectable levels of ACAT1 protein (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ACAT enzymatic activity was stimulated by 25HC in wild-type CHO-K1 cells but not in ACAT1 KO cells.
source: Moreover, ACAT enzymatic activity, as judged by cholesteryl[14C]oleate formation, was stimulated by 25HC, one of the five oxysterols that triggered ACAT activity (Figure 1F), to an expected degree in wild-type (WT) cells but not in ACAT1 KO cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, first two groups), further indicating that the ACAT1 KO cells lacked ACAT activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Stimulation of ACAT enzymatic activity by 25HC was restored by the stable expression of hACAT1(WT), but not hACAT1(H460A) in ACAT1 KO cells.
source: Moreover, stimulation of ACAT enzymatic activity by 25HC was restored by the stable expression of hACAT1(WT), but not hACAT1(H460A) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D last two groups).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Treatment of wild-type CHO-K1 cells with 25HC for 4 hr depleted PM accessible cholesterol in a dose-dependent manner.
source: As expected, treatment of WT cells with 25HC for 4 hr depleted PM accessible cholesterol in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 2A, lanes 1–6, first panel).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: No depletion of PM accessible cholesterol was observed in ACAT1 KO cells after treatment with 25HC for 4 hr.
source: In contrast, no such depletion was observed in ACAT1 KO cells (Figure 2A, lanes 1–6, third panel).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Restoration of ACAT activity by stable expression of hACAT1(WT) reestablished the ability of 25HC to deplete accessible PM cholesterol.
source: Restoration of ACAT activity by stable expression of hACAT1(WT) reestablished the ability of 25HC to deplete accessible PM cholesterol, whereas 25HC had no effect in cells stably expressing an inactive mutant of hACAT1 (H460A) (Figure 2A, lanes 1–6, fifth and seventh panels).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 25HC had no effect on accessible PM cholesterol in cells stably expressing an inactive mutant of hACAT1 (H460A).
source: Restoration of ACAT activity by stable expression of hACAT1(WT) reestablished the ability of 25HC to deplete accessible PM cholesterol, whereas 25HC had no effect in cells stably expressing an inactive mutant of hACAT1 (H460A) (Figure 2A, lanes 1–6, fifth and seventh panels).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Similar dose dependences for suppression of SREBP2 processing by 25HC were observed in all four CHO-K1 cell lines (WT, ACAT1 KO, ACAT1 KO; hACAT1(WT), and ACAT1 KO; hACAT1(H460A)).
source: When each of these four cell lines were depleted of sterols and then treated with 25HC, we observed similar dose dependences for suppression of SREBP2 processing (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), indicating that 25HC entered the cells and reached their ER membranes to bind Insigs and prevent SREBP2 transport.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The inability of 25HC to deplete accessible PM cholesterol in ACAT1 KO cells is not simply due to a defect in cellular entry of 25HC.
source: Thus, the inability of 25HC to deplete accessible PM cholesterol in ACAT1 KO cells is not simply due to a defect in cellular entry of 25HC.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: 4HC did not diminish PM accessible cholesterol in all four CHO-K1 cell lines.
source: In all four cell lines, 4HC did not diminish PM accessible cholesterol (Figure 2A, lane 7, all panels), consistent with this oxysterol's inability to stimulate ACAT activity (Figure 1F, oxysterol A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The four other oxysterols that depleted accessible PM cholesterol in WT cells (oxysterols D, G, H, and J) were unable to do so in the ACAT1 KO cells.
source: Similar to the results with 25HC, the four other oxysterols that depleted accessible PM cholesterol in WT cells (Figure 1D, oxysterols D, G, H, and J) were also unable to do so in the ACAT1 KO cells, further underscoring the link between ACAT and accessible PM cholesterol (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: 25HC treatment for 4 hr eliminated binding of fALOD4-Neon to wild-type CHO-K1 cells, and this effect was abolished in ACAT1 KO cells.
source: Consistent with immunoblot analysis (Figure 2A), we observed that 25HC treatment for 4 hr eliminated binding of fALOD4-Neon to WT cells, and this effect was abolished in ACAT1 KO cells (Figure 2B, top two rows).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Expression of hACAT1(WT), but not hACAT1(H460A), in the ACAT1 KO cells restored 25HC's ability to deplete fALOD4-Neon binding.
source: Likewise, expression of hACAT1(WT), but not hACAT1(H460A), in the ACAT1 KO cells restored 25HC's ability to deplete fALOD4-Neon binding (Figure 2B, third and fourth rows).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In all four CHO-K1 cell lines, binding of fOlyA-647 was unchanged by 25HC treatment.
source: In all four cell lines, binding of fOlyA-647 was unchanged by 25HC treatment (Figure 2B), further highlighting that over a period of 4 hr, 25HC specifically depletes the accessible pool of PM cholesterol in an ACAT-mediated manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Over a period of 4 hr, 25HC specifically depletes the accessible pool of PM cholesterol in an ACAT-mediated manner.
source: In all four cell lines, binding of fOlyA-647 was unchanged by 25HC treatment (Figure 2B), further highlighting that over a period of 4 hr, 25HC specifically depletes the accessible pool of PM cholesterol in an ACAT-mediated manner.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Scap-deficient cells and LXR-deficient cells both had lower levels of accessible cholesterol on their PMs compared to WT cells.
source: Compared to WT cells, Scap-deficient cells (that have no detectable SREBPs) and LXR-deficient cells both had lower levels of accessible cholesterol on their PMs (Figure 2C and D, left panels, lane 1), and this pool of cholesterol was completely depleted by treatment with 25HC for 4 hr (lanes 2–6).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: The accessible cholesterol pool in Scap-deficient cells and LXR-deficient cells was completely depleted by treatment with 25HC for 4 hr.
source: Compared to WT cells, Scap-deficient cells (that have no detectable SREBPs) and LXR-deficient cells both had lower levels of accessible cholesterol on their PMs (Figure 2C and D, left panels, lane 1), and this pool of cholesterol was completely depleted by treatment with 25HC for 4 hr (lanes 2–6).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: Treatment with 4HC had no effect on accessible cholesterol levels in Scap-deficient or LXR-deficient cells.
source: Treatment with 4HC had no effect on accessible cholesterol levels in either Scap- or LXR-deficient cells (Figure 2C and D, left panels, lane 7).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: Levels of SM-sequestered cholesterol in Scap-deficient and LXR-deficient cells were unchanged after treatment with either 25HC or 4HC.
source: Also, levels of SM-sequestered cholesterol in these cells were unchanged after treatment with either 25HC or 4HC (Figure 2C and D, right panels, lanes 1–7).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: The rapid (1–4 hr) removal of accessible cholesterol from PMs by 25HC is due to its activation of ACAT and not due to its modulation of the SREBP or LXR pathways.
source: Combined, the above sets of studies show that the rapid (1–4 hr) removal of accessible cholesterol from PMs by 25HC is due to its activation of ACAT and not due to its modulation of the SREBP or LXR pathways.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The concentration of cholesterol in the PM (~40–50 mole% of total lipids) is almost 10-fold higher than that in the ER membrane (~5 mole% of total lipids).
source: The concentration of cholesterol in the PM (~40–50 mole% of total lipids) is almost 10-fold higher than that in the ER membrane (~5 mole% of total lipids; Lange et al., 1989; Das et al., 2013; Radhakrishnan et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Previous studies have suggested that even though the total cholesterol concentrations in the PM and ER are quite different, the concentration of accessible cholesterol in the two membranes may be similar.
source: Previous studies have suggested that even though the total cholesterol concentrations in the PM and ER are quite different, the concentration of accessible cholesterol in the two membranes may be similar (Lange et al., 2004; Wattenberg and Silbert, 1983; Radhakrishnan and McConnell, 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The equivalence in accessible cholesterol levels between the PM and ER is maintained by rapid bi-directional transport of cholesterol between the two membranes.
source: The equivalence in accessible cholesterol levels between the PM and ER is maintained by rapid bi-directional transport of cholesterol between the two membranes (Lange et al., 1993; Mesmin and Maxfield, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: ACAT activation, and the resulting production of cholesteryl esters, would siphon off some of the accessible cholesterol from the ER, thus lowering levels of accessible cholesterol in the ER relative to the PM.
source: Based on these previous insights, we propose that ACAT activation, and the resulting production of cholesteryl esters, would siphon off some of the accessible cholesterol from the ER, thus lowering levels of accessible cholesterol in the ER relative to the PM.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on prior knowledge and the experimental findings of the study.

claim: Cholesterol transport from the PM to the ER would rapidly restore the equivalence of accessible cholesterol between the two membranes after ACAT activation.
source: Cholesterol transport from the PM to the ER would then rapidly restore the equivalence of accessible cholesterol between the two membranes. As a result, levels of accessible cholesterol in the PM would decline.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on prior knowledge and the experimental findings of the study.

claim: When cells are grown under low cholesterol conditions (lipoprotein-deficient serum, LPDS), both WT and ACAT1 KO cells had the same low levels of accessible and SM-sequestered cholesterol in their PMs.
source: When cells are grown under low cholesterol conditions (lipoprotein-deficient serum, LPDS), ACAT activity is low (Goldstein et al., 1983). Under these conditions, both WT and ACAT1 KO cells had the same low levels of accessible and SM-sequestered cholesterol in their PMs (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and a citation.

claim: When cells are grown under high cholesterol conditions (FCS), the PMs of ACAT1 KO cells had significantly higher levels of accessible cholesterol as compared to WT cells.
source: By comparison, when cells are grown under high cholesterol conditions (FCS), ACAT activity is high (Goldstein et al., 1983). In this case, the PMs of ACAT1 KO cells had significantly higher levels of accessible cholesterol as compared to WT cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and a citation.

claim: There was no difference in levels of SM-sequestered cholesterol in the PMs of WT and ACAT1 KO cells when grown under high cholesterol conditions.
source: Importantly, there was no difference in levels of SM-sequestered cholesterol in the PMs of WT and ACAT1 KO cells (Figure 3B), highlighting the specific effect of the ACAT pathway on accessible PM cholesterol.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In both WT and ACAT1 KO cells, HPCD treatment reduced ER cholesterol levels with similar time dependences.
source: In both WT and ACAT1 KO cells, HPCD treatment reduced ER cholesterol levels with similar time dependences (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), indicating that the pathways that transport cholesterol from ER to PM are not affected in the ACAT1 KO cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The pathways that transport cholesterol from ER to PM are not affected in the ACAT1 KO cells.
source: In both WT and ACAT1 KO cells, HPCD treatment reduced ER cholesterol levels with similar time dependences (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), indicating that the pathways that transport cholesterol from ER to PM are not affected in the ACAT1 KO cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Addition of increasing concentrations of lipoprotein-rich FCS resulted in a similar dose-dependent increase in ER cholesterol in both WT and ACAT1 KO cell lines.
source: We then added back increasing concentrations of lipoprotein-rich FCS and observed a similar dose-dependent increase in ER cholesterol in both cell lines, as judged by reduction of nuclear SREBP2 (Figure 3D, lanes 2–7, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Addition of increasing concentrations of complexes of cholesterol with methyl-β-cyclodextrin (MCD) resulted in a similar dose-dependent increase in ER cholesterol levels in both WT and ACAT1 KO cell lines.
source: Analysis of SREBP2 cleavage in both cell lines showed similar reduction in ER cholesterol levels upon depletion (Figure 3E, lane 1, first and third panels), and a similar dose-dependent increase in ER cholesterol levels upon replenishment with cholesterol/MCD (Figure 3E, lanes 2–6, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The pathways transporting lipoprotein-derived or exogenously added cholesterol from PM to ER are not affected in the ACAT1 KO cells.
source: The results of Figure 3D and E suggest that the pathways transporting lipoprotein-derived or exogenously added cholesterol from PM to ER are not affected in the ACAT1 KO cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: Despite the lack of 25HC in the extracellular media and cells being grown in cholesterol-rich FCS, no replenishment of accessible PM cholesterol was detected even after 22 hr following 25HC removal.
source: We then removed the 25HC and examined accessible PM cholesterol levels over time. Despite the lack of 25HC in the extracellular media and cells being grown in cholesterol-rich FCS, we detected no replenishment of accessible PM cholesterol even after 22 hr (Figure 4A, first panel, lanes 3–8).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: No processing of SREBP2 was detected 22 hr after 25HC removal.
source: In line with our model of equivalence of accessible cholesterol levels in the PM and ER (Figure 3A), we expected that ER accessible cholesterol levels would also be low 22 hr after 25HC removal, which would be reflected in increased cleavage of SREBP2 to its nuclear form. Surprisingly, we detected no processing of SREBP2 (Figure 4A, third panel).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Intracellular 25HC was barely detectable (~0.015 ng/µg of cellular protein) in untreated CHO-K1 cells.
source: Mass spectrometric analysis of intracellular 25HC levels (Figure 4A, bottom panel) showed that 25HC was barely detectable (~0.015 ng/µg of cellular protein) in untreated cells (lane 1) and rose to 4 ng/µg of cellular protein after 25HC treatment for 4 hr (lane 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Intracellular 25HC rose to 4 ng/µg of cellular protein after 25HC treatment for 4 hr.
source: Mass spectrometric analysis of intracellular 25HC levels (Figure 4A, bottom panel) showed that 25HC was barely detectable (~0.015 ng/µg of cellular protein) in untreated cells (lane 1) and rose to 4 ng/µg of cellular protein after 25HC treatment for 4 hr (lane 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: After removal of 25HC from the extracellular medium, the intracellular 25HC declined over the time course of 22 hr to 0.35 ng/µg of cellular protein, a level that was 23-times higher than that in untreated cells and sufficient to suppress SREBP2 cleavage.
source: After removal of 25HC from the extracellular medium, the intracellular 25HC declined over the time course of 22 hr to 0.35 ng/µg of cellular protein (lanes 3–8), a level that was 23-times higher than that in untreated cells and sufficient to suppress SREBP2 cleavage (Figure 4A, lane 8).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: When accessible PM cholesterol was depleted by treatment with HPCD (1 hr), its levels were replenished within 4 hr of HPCD removal.
source: In contrast to the sustained action of 25HC, when accessible PM cholesterol was depleted by treatment with HPCD (1 hr), its levels were replenished within 4 hr of HPCD removal (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, first panel).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: HPCD depletion triggered SREBP2 cleavage in an expected fashion, and this cleavage was suppressed at the same time as an increase in PM accessible cholesterol was detected.
source: Moreover, HPCD depletion triggered SREBP2 cleavage in an expected fashion (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, second panel, lanes 1, 2), and this cleavage was suppressed at the same time as an increase in PM accessible cholesterol was detected (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, second panel, lanes 3–8).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the absence of muristerone, cells had detectable levels of accessible cholesterol in their PMs, which was depleted by 25HC treatment and no replenishment was observed 22 hr after the 25HC was removed.
source: In the absence of muristerone, these cells had detectable levels of accessible cholesterol in their PMs (Figure 4B, lane 1). 25HC treatment depleted this pool and no replenishment was observed 22 hr after the 25HC was removed (Figure 4B, lanes 2, 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: When 25HC was removed, replenishment of accessible cholesterol on the PMs was detected in cells expressing the nuclear forms of SREBP1a and SREBP2, but not SREBP1c.
source: However, when the 25HC was removed, we now detected replenishment of accessible cholesterol on the PMs of cells expressing the nuclear forms of SREBP1a and SREBP2, but not SREBP1c (Figure 4B, lane 6).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The nuclear forms of SREBP1a and SREBP2, but not SREBP1c, increase cholesterol synthesis and induce expression of the LDL receptor allowing for uptake of cholesterol from the LDL in FCS.
source: This isoform specificity for restoring accessible PM cholesterol is consistent with the previous observation that the nuclear forms of SREBP1a and SREBP2, but not SREBP1c, increase cholesterol synthesis and induce expression of the LDL receptor allowing for uptake of cholesterol from the LDL in FCS (Pai et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In the absence of SZ58-035, no replenishment of accessible PM cholesterol was observed after 25HC removal.
source: In the absence of SZ58-035, we observed no replenishment of accessible PM cholesterol (Figure 4C, first panel, lanes 3–8, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In the presence of SZ58-035, accessible cholesterol on PMs began to be detected after 8 hr and ~60% of the initial level of accessible PM cholesterol was restored after 22 hr following 25HC removal.
source: In contrast, in the presence of SZ58-035, we began to detect accessible cholesterol on PMs after 8 hr and ~60% of the initial level of accessible PM cholesterol was restored after 22 hr (Figure 4C, third panel, lanes 3–8, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 25HC acts through two distinct, temporally resolved stages: first, a short pulse of 25HC activates ACAT, which siphons away ER cholesterol resulting in rapid depletion of accessible cholesterol from the PM; second, 25HC's suppression of SREBP-mediated uptake and synthesis of cholesterol combined with continued activation of ACAT, results in sustained depletion of accessible cholesterol in the PM.
source: Based on these data, we hypothesized that 25HC acts through two distinct, temporally resolved stages. First, a short pulse of 25HC activates ACAT, which siphons away ER cholesterol resulting in rapid depletion of accessible cholesterol from the PM. Second, 25HC's suppression of SREBP-mediated uptake and synthesis of cholesterol combined with continued activation of ACAT, results in sustained depletion of accessible cholesterol in the PM.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings of the study.

claim: HPCD treatment (1 hr) induced the depletion of accessible PM cholesterol in both WT and ACAT1 KO cell lines, and this depletion was fully reversed 22 hr after HPCD removal.
source: As expected, HPCD treatment (1 hr) induced the depletion of accessible PM cholesterol in both cell lines (Figure 4D, lanes 1, 2), and this depletion was fully reversed 22 hr after HPCD removal (lane 3), indicating that this mode of cholesterol depletion occurred independently of ACAT activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: HPCD-mediated cholesterol depletion occurred independently of ACAT activity.
source: As expected, HPCD treatment (1 hr) induced the depletion of accessible PM cholesterol in both cell lines (Figure 4D, lanes 1, 2), and this depletion was fully reversed 22 hr after HPCD removal (lane 3), indicating that this mode of cholesterol depletion occurred independently of ACAT activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In WT cells, 25HC depleted the accessible cholesterol and no replenishment was observed after the 25HC was removed.
source: In WT cells, 25HC depleted the accessible cholesterol as expected and no replenishment was observed after the 25HC was removed (Figure 4D, first panel, lanes 4, 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In ACAT1 KO cells, 25HC did not deplete accessible PM cholesterol and there was no further change after the 25HC was removed.
source: However, in ACAT1 KO cells, 25HC did not deplete accessible PM cholesterol and there was no further change after the 25HC was removed (Figure 4D, third panel, lanes 4, 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Without the initial action of 25HC on ACAT, the lingering intracellular 25HC that inhibits new cholesterol synthesis and uptake through suppressing SREBP activation is not enough to reduce accessible PM cholesterol, even after 22 hr.
source: Thus, without the initial action of 25HC on ACAT, the lingering intracellular 25HC that inhibits new cholesterol synthesis and uptake through suppressing SREBP activation is not enough to reduce accessible PM cholesterol, even after 22 hr.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Recent studies have indicated that 25HC protects cells from pore-forming activities of bacterial cholesterol-dependent cytolysins (CDCs) that exploit accessible PM cholesterol.
source: Recent studies have indicated that 25HC protects cells from pore-forming activities of bacterial cholesterol-dependent cytolysins (CDCs) that exploit accessible PM cholesterol (Zhou et al., 2020; Ormsby et al., 2022; Ormsby et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Much lower concentrations of ALO were required to form pores in ACAT1 KO cells compared to WT cells.
source: Dose curve analysis showed that much lower concentrations of ALO were required to form pores in ACAT1 KO cells compared to WT cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, left panel), consistent with the higher amounts of accessible cholesterol in the PMs of ACAT1 KO cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Stable expression of hACAT1(WT), but not inactive hACAT1(H460A), in the ACAT1 KO cells rendered them less susceptible to pore formation by ALO.
source: Moreover, stable expression of hACAT1(WT), but not inactive hACAT1(H460A), in the ACAT1 KO cells rendered them less susceptible to pore formation by ALO (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, right panel).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 25HC treatment of WT cells abolished pore formation by ALO and PFO in a dose-dependent manner.
source: As expected, 25HC treatment of WT cells abolished pore formation by ALO and PFO in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 5, first column), consistent with 25HC's ability to deplete accessible cholesterol from the PMs of these cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: 25HC treatment had no effect on pore formation in ACAT1 KO cells due to its inability to deplete accessible cholesterol from the PMs of these cells.
source: In contrast, 25HC treatment had no effect on pore formation in ACAT1 KO cells (Figure 5, second column) due to its inability to deplete accessible cholesterol from the PMs of these cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Restoration of ACAT activity by stable expression of hACAT1(WT) reestablished the ability of 25HC to abolish pore formation, whereas inactive hACAT1(H460A) was unable to do so.
source: Restoration of ACAT activity by stable expression of hACAT1(WT) reestablished the ability of 25HC to abolish pore formation, whereas inactive hACAT1(H460A) was unable to do so (Figure 5, third and fourth columns).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: In all four cell lines, 4HC had no effects on pore formation.
source: In all four cell lines, 4HC had no effects on pore formation (Figure 5), consistent with this oxysterol's inability to deplete accessible cholesterol from PMs (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The protective effects of 25HC on macrophage lysis by CDCs primarily relies on ACAT activation.
source: The above data obtained with ACAT1 KO CHO-K1 cells indicates that the protective effects of 25HC on macrophage lysis by CDCs primarily relies on ACAT activation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Accessible cholesterol is required for Listeria to form membrane protrusions at cellular junctions and spread into neighboring cells.
source: We have previously shown that accessible cholesterol is required for Listeria to form membrane protrusions at cellular junctions and spread into neighboring cells, and that 25HC treatment for 18 hr blocks this spread (Abrams et al., 2020a; Abrams et al., 2020b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: 25HC treatment for 18 hr blocks the spread of Listeria into neighboring cells.
source: We have previously shown that accessible cholesterol is required for Listeria to form membrane protrusions at cellular junctions and spread into neighboring cells, and that 25HC treatment for 18 hr blocks this spread (Abrams et al., 2020a; Abrams et al., 2020b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The increased accessible PM cholesterol in ACAT1 KO cells did not affect invasion or cell-to-cell spread of Listeria as similar levels of infection were observed in both WT and ACAT1 KO cells after 22 hr.
source: The increased accessible PM cholesterol in ACAT1 KO cells did not affect invasion or cell-to-cell spread of Listeria as similar levels of infection were observed in both WT and ACAT1 KO cells after 22 hr (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Short-term incubation of WT cells with 25HC prior to infection (followed by removal of the oxysterol) reduced Listeria infection in a dose dependent manner.
source: In contrast to these results, short-term incubation of WT cells with 25HC prior to infection (followed by removal of the oxysterol) reduced Listeria infection in a dose dependent manner (Figure 6A, first column), but this treatment had no effect on infection of ACAT1 KO cells (Figure 6A, second column).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Short-term incubation with 25HC prior to infection had no effect on infection of ACAT1 KO cells.
source: In contrast to these results, short-term incubation of WT cells with 25HC prior to infection (followed by removal of the oxysterol) reduced Listeria infection in a dose dependent manner (Figure 6A, first column), but this treatment had no effect on infection of ACAT1 KO cells (Figure 6A, second column).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The antibacterial activity of 25HC was restored by expression of hACAT1(WT), whereas inactive hACAT1(H460A) did not reduce infection.
source: The antibacterial activity of 25HC was restored by expression of hACAT1(WT), whereas inactive hACAT1(H460A) did not reduce infection (Figure 6A, third and fourth columns).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In all four cell lines, 4HC had no effects on Listeria infection.
source: In all four cell lines, 4HC had no effects on Listeria infection (Figure 6A), consistent with this oxysterol's inability to deplete accessible cholesterol from PMs (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Genetic ablation of cholesterol 25-hydroxylase (Ch25h), the enzyme that produces 25HC, in mice enhanced the transmission of Listeria from the gut to the spleen.
source: Previously, we showed that genetic ablation of cholesterol 25-hydroxylase (Ch25h), the enzyme that produces 25HC, in mice enhanced the transmission of Listeria from the gut to the spleen, and that delivery of exogenous 25HC suppressed this systemic transmission (Abrams et al., 2020a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Delivery of exogenous 25HC suppressed the systemic transmission of Listeria from the gut to the spleen in mice.
source: Previously, we showed that genetic ablation of cholesterol 25-hydroxylase (Ch25h), the enzyme that produces 25HC, in mice enhanced the transmission of Listeria from the gut to the spleen, and that delivery of exogenous 25HC suppressed this systemic transmission (Abrams et al., 2020a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Transmission of Lm-InlAm to liver and spleen tissues was significantly reduced in wild-type mice treated with 25HC.
source: Consistent with our previous studies, transmission of Lm-InlAm to liver and spleen tissues was significantly reduced in wild-type mice treated with 25HC (Figure 6B, top row).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: 25HC was unable to protect ACAT1 KO mice from Lm-InlAm infection.
source: However, 25HC was unable to protect ACAT1 KO mice from Lm-InlAm infection (Figure 6B, bottom row).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: No difference in Lm-InlAm levels was observed in the caecal tissues of wild-type and ACAT1 KO mice upon 25HC treatment.
source: In contrast to what we observed in liver and spleen tissues, we observed no difference in Lm-InlAm levels in the caecal tissues of wild-type and ACAT1 KO mice upon 25HC treatment (Figure 6B), indicating that 25HC protects the organism from systemic transmission and not initial bacterial invasion of the gut epithelium.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: 25HC protects the organism from systemic transmission of Listeria and not initial bacterial invasion of the gut epithelium.
source: In contrast to what we observed in liver and spleen tissues, we observed no difference in Lm-InlAm levels in the caecal tissues of wild-type and ACAT1 KO mice upon 25HC treatment (Figure 6B), indicating that 25HC protects the organism from systemic transmission and not initial bacterial invasion of the gut epithelium.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: 25HC elicits long-term protective effects in vivo through activation of ACAT.
source: These data are consistent with those obtained in cultured cells and provide evidence that 25HC elicits long-term protective effects in vivo through activation of ACAT.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: 25HC has been shown to suppress highly pathogenic viruses including human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), Ebola virus, Nipah virus, Rift Valley fever virus, Zika virus (ZIKV), and SARS-CoV-2, the causative agent of COVID-19.
source: 25HC has also been shown to suppress highly pathogenic viruses including human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), Ebola virus, Nipah virus, Rift Valley fever virus, Zika virus (ZIKV), and SARS-CoV-2, the causative agent of COVID-19 (Wang et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2013; Li et al., 2017; Zu et al., 2020; Zang et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: ACAT activity in Huh7.5 cells arises from two isoforms of ACAT, ACAT1 and ACAT2.
source: Unlike the CHO-K1 cells used above, ACAT activity in Huh7.5 cells arises from two isoforms of ACAT, ACAT1 and ACAT2 (Pramfalk et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: ACAT enzymatic activity was stimulated by 25HC in Huh7.5 cells but not in Huh7.5ΔACAT cells.
source: ACAT enzymatic activity, as judged by cholesteryl [14C]oleate formation, was stimulated by 25HC to an expected degree in Huh7.5 cells but not in Huh7.5ΔACAT cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 25HC was unable to deplete accessible cholesterol from the PMs of the Huh7.5ΔACAT cells.
source: Consistent with the diminished ACAT activity, 25HC was unable to deplete accessible cholesterol from the PMs of the Huh7.5ΔACAT cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The ability of ZIKV to infect Huh7.5ΔACAT cells was increased by 60% compared to infection of Huh7.5 cells.
source: The ability of ZIKV to infect Huh7.5ΔACAT cells was increased by 60% compared to infection of Huh7.5 cells (Figure 7A, middle and right panels, gray bars).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: hCoV-OC43 infection of Huh7.5ΔACAT cells was reduced by 45% compared to infection of Huh7.5 cells.
source: In contrast, hCoV-OC43 infection of Huh7.5ΔACAT cells was reduced by 45% compared to infection of Huh7.5 cells (Figure 7B, middle and right panel, gray bars).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: 25HC treatment for 4 hr reduced ZIKV infection by 48% in Huh7.5 cells.
source: 25HC treatment for 4 hr reduced ZIKV and hCoV-OC43 infection by 48% and 57%, respectively (Figure 7A and B, middle panels, orange bars).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: 25HC treatment for 4 hr reduced hCoV-OC43 infection by 57% in Huh7.5 cells.
source: 25HC treatment for 4 hr reduced ZIKV and hCoV-OC43 infection by 48% and 57%, respectively (Figure 7A and B, middle panels, orange bars).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The protective effect of 25HC toward both ZIKV and hCoV-OC43 was severely attenuated in the Huh7.5ΔACAT cells.
source: Strikingly, the protective effect of 25HC toward both viruses was severely attenuated in the Huh7.5ΔACAT cells (Figure 7A and B, right panels, orange bars).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7A and 7B.

claim: Treatment with 4HC did not alter ZIKV or hCoV-OC43 infection in Huh7.5 or Huh7.5ΔACAT cells.
source: In all cases, treatment with 4HC did not alter infection (Figure 7A and B, blue bars).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7A and 7B.

claim: Accessible cholesterol was depleted from the PMs of Huh7.5 cells, but not Huh7.5ΔACAT cells, by 25HC treatment for 4 hr.
